title: Stage 3: Envelope encryption
summary: Give every entry its own random data key, wrap only that key with the master key, and change the master password without re-encrypting a single entry.

steps.title: Stage 3: a key per entry
body: In stage 2, changing the password would mean decrypting and re-encrypting every secret. Real systems avoid that with **envelope encryption**: each entry gets its own random **data key** (DEK), and only the DEK is encrypted (**wrapped**) with the master key, which now acts as a **key-encryption key** (KEK).
`put <name> <secret>` now:
1. `dek = RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(32)` (random for real; it is never printed, so tests stay deterministic)
2. seal the secret with the **DEK**: nonce = `NextNonce()`, associated data = the name
3. wrap the DEK with the **master key**: nonce = `NextNonce()` (the *next* counter value), associated data = `"dek:" + name`
4. store all six pieces: `Entry(Nonce, Cipher, Tag, KeyNonce, WrappedKey, KeyTag)` and wipe the DEK

`get` unwraps the DEK, then opens the data. A failure in either step prints `error: <name> has been tampered with`. The output of `put`, `get`, `list`, `tamper` and `swap` is unchanged, but `dump` now shows the envelope, because the data ciphertext depends on a random key:
```text
nonce=<data nonce hex> key-nonce=<key nonce hex> ct=<n> bytes wrapped=48 bytes
(`wrapped` counts the 32-byte wrapped key plus its 16-byte tag.)

steps.prompt: A user changes their master password on a vault with 10,000 entries. With envelope encryption, what must be re-encrypted?
options: Only the 10,000 small wrapped data keys; the entries' ciphertexts stay exactly as they are
Nothing at all: the old wrapped keys keep working
steps.explain: Each wrapped key is 48 bytes, whatever the size of the secret. That is why cloud KMS, disk encryption and databases all use envelopes: rotating the key at the top is cheap.

steps.title: Changing the password
body: Two new commands:
| Command | Prints |
| `tamper-key <name>` | `tampered <name>`, after flipping bit 0 of `WrappedKey[0]` |
| `passwd <old> <new>` | `password changed (key-check <8 hex>, rewrapped <n> data keys)` |
`passwd` works whether the vault is locked or not, and in this order:
1. no vault: `error: no vault`; no new password: `error: missing argument`
2. derive the old key and check it against the key-check: `error: wrong password`
3. new password under 8 characters: `error: password too short`
4. **unwrap every DEK first**, in ordinal name order. If one fails: `error: <name> has been tampered with`, and *nothing* changes
5. derive the new key, then re-wrap each DEK (ordinal order, a fresh `NextNonce()` each) with the new key
6. replace the key-check, keep the vault unlocked with the new key
Doing all the unwrapping before any rewrapping is what makes the change all-or-nothing: you never end up with half the entries under each password.

steps.prompt: Arrange the body of `put` for an envelope-encrypted entry.
lines: var (cipher, tag) = Seal(dek, NextNonce(), Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(secret), name);
var (wrapped, keyTag) = Seal(masterKey, keyNonce, dek, "dek:" + name);
steps.explain: The DEK must exist before it can encrypt or be wrapped, the data takes the first nonce and the wrap the second, and the plaintext key is wiped once it is safely wrapped.

steps.prompt: The vault in this stage, given these commands, prints its `dump` lines. What is the **key-nonce** of entry `a` after the password change? Type the 24 hex characters.
code: // passwd  -> rewraps a, then b, in ordinal name order
steps.explain: `a` sorts before `b`, so it is rewrapped first with counter 5. Its *data* nonce stays 3: the ciphertext was never touched.

steps.title: Wrap data keys
prompt: Switch `put`, `get` and `dump` to envelope encryption, and add `tamper-key` and `passwd`, as specified on the two cards above. Everything from stages 1 and 2 must keep working.
password changed (key-check c219dde2, rewrapped 2 data keys)
starter: // Tests only: a real vault uses 600,000+ iterations and a random salt stored next to the vault.
byte[]? keyCheck;    // stored with the vault: proves a password is right without storing the key
byte[]? masterKey;   // only in memory, only while unlocked
ulong counter;       // last nonce used under the master key; never goes backwards
string Arg(int i) => i < parts.Length ? parts[i] : "";
"status" => keyCheck is null ? "no vault" : masterKey is null ? "locked" : "unlocked",
static byte[] KeyCheck(byte[] key) => HMACSHA256.HashData(key, Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("key-check"));
if (keyCheck is not null) return "error: vault already exists";
if (keyCheck is null) return "error: no vault";
if (keyCheck is null) return "error: no vault";
var nonce = new byte[12];                                  // 4 zero bytes, then the counter
// AES-GCM in one place. Open returns null when the tag does not verify.
static (byte[] Cipher, byte[] Tag) Seal(byte[] key, byte[] nonce, byte[] plain, string aad)
static byte[]? Open(byte[] key, byte[] nonce, byte[] cipher, byte[] tag, string aad)
var (cipher, tag) = Seal(masterKey, nonce, Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(secret), name);
if (!entries.TryGetValue(name, out var e)) return $"error: no entry {name}";
var plain = Open(masterKey, e.Nonce, e.Cipher, e.Tag, name);
return plain is null ? $"error: {name} has been tampered with" : $"{name}: {Encoding.UTF8.GetString(plain)}";
if (!entries.TryGetValue(name, out var e)) return $"error: no entry {name}";
e.Cipher[0] ^= 1;                                          // an attacker flips one bit on disk
record Entry(byte[] Nonce, byte[] Cipher, byte[] Tag);
solution: // Tests only: a real vault uses 600,000+ iterations and a random salt stored next to the vault.
byte[]? keyCheck;    // stored with the vault: proves a password is right without storing the key
byte[]? masterKey;   // only in memory, only while unlocked
ulong counter;       // last nonce used; never goes backwards, so no nonce repeats under any key
string Arg(int i) => i < parts.Length ? parts[i] : "";
"status" => keyCheck is null ? "no vault" : masterKey is null ? "locked" : "unlocked",
static byte[] KeyCheck(byte[] key) => HMACSHA256.HashData(key, Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("key-check"));
if (keyCheck is not null) return "error: vault already exists";
if (keyCheck is null) return "error: no vault";
if (keyCheck is null) return "error: no vault";
var nonce = new byte[12];                                  // 4 zero bytes, then the counter
// AES-GCM in one place. Open returns null when the tag does not verify.
static (byte[] Cipher, byte[] Tag) Seal(byte[] key, byte[] nonce, byte[] plain, string aad)
static byte[]? Open(byte[] key, byte[] nonce, byte[] cipher, byte[] tag, string aad)
// Envelope encryption: each entry has its own random data key (DEK), and only the
// DEK is encrypted ("wrapped") with the master key.
var (cipher, tag) = Seal(dek, nonce, Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(secret), name);
var (wrapped, keyTag) = Seal(masterKey, keyNonce, dek, "dek:" + name);
entries[name] = new Entry(nonce, cipher, tag, keyNonce, wrapped, keyTag);
byte[]? Unwrap(byte[] kek, string name, Entry e) => Open(kek, e.KeyNonce, e.WrappedKey, e.KeyTag, "dek:" + name);
if (!entries.TryGetValue(name, out var e)) return $"error: no entry {name}";
if (dek is null) return $"error: {name} has been tampered with";
var plain = Open(dek, e.Nonce, e.Cipher, e.Tag, name);
return plain is null ? $"error: {name} has been tampered with" : $"{name}: {Encoding.UTF8.GetString(plain)}";
if (!entries.TryGetValue(name, out var e)) return $"error: no entry {name}";
e.Cipher[0] ^= 1;                                          // an attacker flips one bit on disk
if (!entries.TryGetValue(name, out var e)) return $"error: no entry {name}";
// Changing the password re-wraps every data key. The entries themselves are not touched.
if (keyCheck is null) return "error: no vault";
if (dek is null) return $"error: {name} has been tampered with";
var (wrapped, keyTag) = Seal(newKey, keyNonce, dek, "dek:" + name);
entries[name] = entries[name] with { KeyNonce = keyNonce, WrappedKey = wrapped, KeyTag = keyTag };
record Entry(byte[] Nonce, byte[] Cipher, byte[] Tag, byte[] KeyNonce, byte[] WrappedKey, byte[] KeyTag);

tests.name: dump shows the envelope
tests.stdin:
init correct-horse
put github ghp_secret123
put email hunter2
dump github
dump email

tests.name: tampering with data or with a wrapped key
tests.stdin:
init correct-horse
put a one
put b two
tamper a
tamper-key b
get a
get b
expect: error: a has been tampered with
error: b has been tampered with

tests.name: passwd rewraps keys and leaves data alone
tests.stdin:
init correct-horse
put b x1
put a y2
dump a
passwd correct-horse battery-staple
dump a
dump b
get a
get b
lock
unlock correct-horse
unlock battery-staple
status
expect: password changed (key-check c219dde2, rewrapped 2 data keys)

tests.name: passwd refuses bad input and changes nothing
tests.stdin:
init correct-horse
passwd wrong-horse new-password-1
passwd correct-horse short
put a x
tamper-key a
passwd correct-horse battery-staple
lock
unlock battery-staple
unlock correct-horse
expect: error: a has been tampered with

tests.stdin:

list

require.message: Generates each data key with RandomNumberGenerator
Stores a wrapped data key with each entry

hints: Add `KeyNonce`, `WrappedKey` and `KeyTag` to the `Entry` record, and an `Unwrap(byte[] kek, string name, Entry e)` helper that returns `null` on failure.
In `passwd`, collect every unwrapped DEK into a dictionary first; return the tamper error before touching anything.
Update an entry with `entries[name] = entries[name] with { KeyNonce = ..., WrappedKey = ..., KeyTag = ... };`.
